articles.title: Pentagon data breach exposes records of over 3M people
articles.summary: The Pentagon data breach exposed 2.76 million Social Security numbers and military records, raising long-term identity theft concerns for veterans.
articles.body: You can change a password after a breach. You can cancel a credit card. But when your Social Security number gets exposed, you could be dealing with the fallout for years. That is the concern after a major breach involving the Pentagon's Defense Manpower Data Center. If you have served in the military, worked for the Department of War or have other ties to the military community, your information could be among the records involved. A War Department official told CyberGuy that 2.76 million living individuals and 294,000 deceased individuals were affected. Depending on the person, the exposed information can include Social Security numbers, names, dates of birth, contact information and military personnel details. So, if a breach letter from the Pentagon shows up in your mailbox, don't toss it aside. Here's what happened, what may have been exposed and what you can do to protect yourself. DMV BREACH CONFIRMED AS HACKERS CLAIM 200,000 RECORDS STOLEN Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com How the Pentagon data breach happened The breach involved the Defense Manpower Data Center, or DMDC. A War Department official told CyberGuy that a DMDC information system experienced unauthorized access to personally identifiable information by a small number of unauthorized users between October 2025 and July 2026. The official said DMDC immediately remediated the vulnerability after discovering it. At this time, the department says it has no indication that the accessed information has been misused. The files accessed contained unencrypted personally identifiable information. That created a potentially long exposure window before the vulnerability was discovered. Personal information such as a Social Security number can remain useful to criminals long after the original breach fades from the headlines. What information was exposed in the Pentagon breach The specific information varies depending on the person. According to the Pentagon, exposed records can include: The military details make this breach particularly sensitive because the records may reveal more than basic identity information. DMDC plays a major role behind the scenes at the Department of Defense. It maintains more than 60 million records covering military personnel, civilian employees, contractors, family members, retirees and veterans. The agency uses those records to support benefits, identity verification and other Defense Department programs. In other words, plenty of people who left active military service years ago may still have information stored in these systems. How to know if the Pentagon breach affected you People whose personal information was accessed are being notified by postal mail through the Department's contracted provider, Identity Theft Guard Solutions, or IDX. If you receive a notice, read it carefully rather than assuming it is another piece of junk mail. The letter should explain what information tied to you was affected and what protection is being offered. According to the War Department official, IDX is providing notification, credit monitoring and identity restoration support based on the data elements affected for each individual. Anyone with questions can visit response.idx.us/DMDC or call 1-855-744-4556. Be careful with unexpected emails or text messages claiming to be connected to the breach. Scammers can use major security incidents as an excuse to send fake notices or links designed to steal even more information. Instead of clicking a link in an unexpected message, verify the information using the official IDX contact details or the postal notice you received. WHY SCAMMERS TARGET VETERANS AND HOW TO FIGHT BACK Why stolen Social Security numbers create a long-term risk A credit card number has an expiration date. Your Social Security number usually stays with you for life. That can give criminals plenty of time to combine stolen information from one breach with information collected elsewhere. Someone might already have your phone number or an old email address. Adding a Social Security number and date of birth can make a stolen identity far more useful. A criminal could try to open credit in your name or use the information in a convincing phishing attack. Other forms of identity fraud may never involve your credit report at all. That is why I would treat a breach involving an SSN differently from one exposing an email address or password. What to do if your information was exposed A breach notice can leave you wondering where to start, so focus first on the protections that can limit what someone does with the information. 1) Enroll in the free monitoring if you are eligible If DMDC sent you an official notification, review the identity protection services available to you. Eligible individuals may receive 12 months of free credit monitoring and identity restoration support through IDX, depending on the information affected. Credit monitoring can warn you about certain changes to your credit file. However, monitoring usually alerts you after activity occurs. It does not stop someone from attempting to use your identity. If you were not contacted by DMDC, or if you want protection that continues beyond the free 12-month period, you may also want to consider a broader identity theft protection service. Depending on the service, it may monitor for suspicious use of your personal information and provide help if identity theft occurs. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com. 2) Freeze your credit Consider placing a credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze restricts access to your credit file, which can make it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name. You can temporarily lift the freeze when you legitimately need to apply for credit. A freeze remains one of the strongest free steps you can take after your Social Security number has been exposed. Keep in mind that a freeze focuses on new credit. It cannot stop every type of identity theft, including fraud involving an existing account. 3) Consider placing a fraud alert If you do not want to freeze your credit, you can place a fraud alert on your credit reports. A fraud alert tells lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening new credit. You only need to contact one of the three major credit bureaus, and that bureau should notify the other two. A fraud alert offers less protection than a freeze, but it can still add another layer of scrutiny. PENTAGON DATA BREACH EXPOSES SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBERS, PERSONAL INFO OF 2.76M US MILITARY, CIVILIAN PERSONNEL 4) Watch your existing accounts Review your bank and credit card activity regularly. Also pay attention to unexpected changes involving accounts that use your identity. Turn on transaction alerts where available. Quick warnings can help you spot activity before it grows into a bigger problem. 5) Be suspicious of messages about the breach and use strong antivirus software Scammers pay attention to major data breaches too. You could receive a call, email or text from someone claiming to represent the Defense Department, a credit monitoring company or another organization offering to help you secure your identity. Do not hand over a Social Security number, password or verification code because someone contacts you unexpectedly. Also avoid opening attachments or clicking links in unexpected breach-related messages. Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads, suspicious links and other threats that may show up in follow-up scams. Keep your security software updated and verify unexpected requests using official contact information you find yourself. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 6) Protect important accounts with two-factor authentication Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email, financial accounts and other important services whenever it is available. Your email account deserves special attention because criminals can use it to reset passwords for other accounts. An authenticator app or passkey can offer stronger protection than relying only on a password. 7) Get an IRS Identity Protection PIN If your Social Security number was exposed, consider getting an IRS Identity Protection PIN. An IP PIN is a six-digit number that helps prevent someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number. The IRS issues a new PIN each year. This can be especially useful after a breach because tax-related identity theft may not show up on a credit report. 8) Keep watching after the free monitoring ends One year of free monitoring is useful, but stolen personal information does not become harmless when that year expires. Continue checking your credit reports and financial accounts. Also pay attention to unexpected tax notices, benefit claims or bills that you do not recognize. We have previously explained why a credit freeze alone does not stop every form of identity theft. A stolen Social Security number can potentially be misused in ways that never trigger a traditional credit check. Kurt's key takeaways What stands out to me here is how long the information involved can remain valuable. A password can be replaced in a few minutes, but a Social Security number, birth date or military history can follow you for decades. If you receive one of these Pentagon breach notices, I would take it seriously even though officials say they have not seen evidence of misuse. Use the free monitoring being offered and consider freezing your credit. Then keep an eye on your accounts after that free monitoring period ends. We hand organizations an enormous amount of personal information because we often have no practical alternative. When that information gets exposed, the burden of watching for fraud suddenly falls back on us. If the government loses information as sensitive as your Social Security number, should it be responsible for protecting your identity for longer than one year? articles.title: Flood damaged EVs pose fire risk even after water recedes, fire officials say
articles.summary: Saltwater can damage lithium-ion batteries found in electric vehicles, hybrids, electric bicycles and scooters, potentially triggering fires days or even weeks after the initial exposure.
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — Following coastal flooding in Southern California this week, fire officials are warning residents about a potentially dangerous consequence of saltwater exposure involving electric vehicles and other battery-powered transportation.

The Laguna Beach Fire Department said saltwater can damage lithium-ion batteries found in electric vehicles, hybrids, electric bicycles and scooters, potentially triggering fires days or even weeks after the initial exposure.

Flash flood warnings have been issued for portions of Orange, Riverside and Imperial counties as a result of post-Tropical Storm Rachel moving through the region and bringing widespread coastal flooding.

The storm has already battered coastal communities, including Long Beach, Newport Beach and Malibu, where powerful waves and unusually high tides have flooded streets, damaged infrastructure and prompted emergency measures.

In Long Beach, mandatory evacuations were ordered for homes along portions of Seaside Walk after several structures were deemed unsafe to occupy.

Along the Los Angeles County coastline, a coastal flood warning remained in effect until 3 p.m. Sunday, with forecasters warning that high tides approaching 8 feet and surf of 5 to 8 feet could produce significant flooding and beach erosion.

Officials warned that even vehicles that appear to be operating normally could pose a fire risk if floodwater reached their batteries or electrical components.

Residents who suspect their vehicle sustained saltwater damage, including those whose vehicles were partially submerged, are urged not to drive or charge them.

Instead, fire officials recommend contacting their insurance company, arranging for professional towing and having the vehicle inspected by a certified mechanic qualified to service electric or hybrid vehicles.

The warning also applies to e-bikes and electric scooters that may have been exposed to coastal floodwaters.

According to the department, warning signs of a potentially dangerous battery include smoke, hissing or popping sounds and unusual heat.

Anyone noticing those signs should immediately move away from the vehicle and call 911.

Officials cautioned residents against attempting to move a vehicle exhibiting those warning signs or trying to extinguish a battery fire themselves.

The department emphasized that the danger may not be immediately apparent, with battery fires potentially occurring long after floodwaters have receded.

KTLA Digital Producer Lily Dallow contributed to this report.

articles.title: Delta postpones Atlanta-to-Riyadh service after Houthi attacks on Saudi airport
articles.summary: Delta Air Lines said Monday it will postpone the launch of its flight service from Atlanta to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched deadly attacks on the latter city’s King Khalid International Airport. Citing “evolving developments in the region,” Delta said in a release it was delaying the launch until March. The…
articles.body:
Delta Air Lines said Monday it will postpone the launch of its flight service from Atlanta to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched deadly attacks on the latter city’s King Khalid International Airport.

Citing “evolving developments in the region,” Delta said in a release it was delaying the launch until March. The nonstop flight service from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport to Riyadh was scheduled to start on Oct. 23.

“The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions. We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation,” the company continued, referencing two Saudi-based airlines.

Delta noted that Saudi Arabia “remains an important market” for the company, adding it is “committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term.”

The weekend’s attacks on King Khalid resulted in the deaths of at least 13 people, including four Saudi citizens, one American, two Bangladeshi nationals, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Pakistani national , one Palestinian, one Sudanese national and one Syrian, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).

The attacks, which the Houthis carried out on Saturday and Sunday, also injured at least 320 others, GACA reported. The aviation authority has suspended operations at the airport, located in the Saudi capital.

Airlines have canceled nearly 550 flights to and from King Khalid over the past 24 hours, according to data from FlightAware .

Before Delta announced the postponement of its Atlanta-to-Riyadh service launch, CEO Ed Bastian told CNBC on Monday that “safety” would dictate the company’s decision.

“Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week,” Bastian added.

The Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday advised U.S. pilots to “exercise caution” when flying in Saudi airspace due to risks associated with “ongoing military activities.” The notice is in effect until Dec. 10.

The State Department also advises Americans to “reconsider” travel to Saudi Arabia due to the risk of drone and missile attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis, a Yemeni rebel group.

U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia need “special authorization” to use any airport in Saudi Arabia and cannot travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border due to safety risks, the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh wrote Monday on social platform X.

articles.title: US military archbishop: Streamed execution threatens to ‘imitate the terrorists’
articles.summary: Archbishop Timothy Broglio, head of the Archdiocese for the Military Services, on Monday said he does not approve of the Trump administration’s decision to livestream the military execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, warning that it could “imitate the terrorists.” Broglio said in a statement released by the Archdiocese for the Military…
articles.body:
Archbishop Timothy Broglio, head of the Archdiocese for the Military Services, on Monday said he does not approve of the Trump administration’s decision to livestream the military execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, warning that it could “imitate the terrorists.”

Broglio said in a statement released by the Archdiocese for the Military Services that he sends his sympathy to the families and friends of Fort Hood shooting victims, noting that he presided over the funeral of one of those killed, Michael Grant Cahill.

He added that he sides with the Catholic Church’s opposition to capital punishment, “and Pope Francis made it even clearer.”

“Thirdly, do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries?” he continued. “The crime committed by Nidal Malik Hasan was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?”

“Has the potential moral injury, which the members of the firing squad might experience, been considered?” Broglio inquired. “Will the exposure of a livestream to the young and impressionable during the 250th anniversary year of our independence be able to be repaired?”

He asked if there was any “value” in having the U.S. military thrown “in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world.”

“Does this decision reflect the dignity of the human person?” Broglio said before calling on service members to stop the livestream and urging Catholic members of the firing squad “to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the church.”

When asked by The Hill about Broglio’s remarks, the Pentagon referred to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s response to a CBS News social media post about the execution being livestreamed. His short response reads: “Correct.”

Hegseth on Thursday announced that the former U.S. Army major’s execution will be streamed and open to the public for viewing. The execution falls on Dec. 3, a Thursday, the same day of the week Hasan had planned his attack. It will also be held at Fort Hood, Hegseth said.

The announcement drew condemnation over its publicity. Democratic and Republican lawmakers urged the Pentagon to reverse its decision, with Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) warning that the stream could potentially fuel radicalization.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the choice , saying on Sunday that it is part of President Trump “restoring American values.” He dismissed concerns that it could fuel radicalization.

“I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime,” Mullin said on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.” “I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies.”

articles.title: Oil prices spike after Houthi attacks on Saudi airports
articles.summary: Oil prices rose Monday, after the Iranian-backed Houthis launched attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia over the weekend. articles.body:
Oil prices rose Monday, after the Iranian-backed Houthis launched attacks on two airports in Saudi Arabia over the weekend.

Brent Crude, the international benchmark, closed at nearly $106 per barrel as of late Monday afternoon, up roughly $1.20 from closing time Friday. The price of Brent Crude peaked at $107.33 earlier in the day.

West Texas Intermediate Crude, the North American standard, reached $94.36 during Monday trading and closed at $93.16 per barrel .

The Houthis, a Yemen-based rebel group aligned with Iran, launched a string of attacks over the weekend on King Khalid International Airport and King Fahd International Airport , respectively located in Riyadh and Dammam, Saudi Arabia.

The pair of attacks on King Khalid killed at least 13 people and injured at least 320 others, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). GACA noted Sunday it was assessing the damage of the attack on King Fahd International Airport, which resulted in injuries.

President Trump said Saturday the U.S. “may” join Saudi Arabia in responding to the Houthis.

“We will make a decision. We move very quickly,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

Saudi forces, which the Obama administration and first Trump administration supplied with offensive weapons , have fought against the Houthis in Yemen for more than a decade.

The Iranian proxy group has continued to launch strikes into the kingdom during the U.S.-Iran war . The latter conflict, in its eighth month, has led to oil price spikes stemming from the Islamic Republic’s restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The shock to the energy industry has increased prices at the pump back home. As of Monday, a gallon of regular gas costs roughly $4.36 on average nationally, up about $1.28 from a year ago, according to data from AAA .

A gallon of diesel fuel also costs around $2.60 more on average than it did a year ago, AAA reported.

Trump on Friday announced a deal for Russia to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets, in an attempt to lower prices ahead of the midterms.

Under the deal, Russia will “immediately” supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the marketplaces, before supplying another 500,000 tons next month, 1 million tons “immediately thereafter” and 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” depending on the condition of its diesel refineries, Trump wrote on Truth Social .

But analysts cautioned the deal may not lower prices, with GasBuddy’s Patrick De Haan saying Monday he was “skeptical” it will “deliver significant relief to the trucking industry and consumers who depend on diesel.”

articles.title: Trump Floats Potential Meeting With Kim Jong Un During Asia Trip
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during an upcoming trip to Asia, stoking speculation about renewed US outreach...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said he might meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during an upcoming trip to Asia, stoking speculation about renewed US outreach to the reclusive regime.

"I may," Trump told reporters Monday when asked if he would meet with Kim during his trip. "That would be exciting."

Trump is slated to travel next month to the region, where he's expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

Trump has raised the prospect of another meeting with Kim in recent weeks, indicating he would like it to happen this year. The two leaders met thrice during the US president's first term, though those discussions failed to produce any diplomatic breakthroughs.

Still, Trump has repeatedly touted what he describes as warm relations between him and Kim. "I get along with him," Trump said on Monday.

Earlier this month, Trump also met with basketball star Dennis Rodman, who has traveled to North Korea multiple times and has had an unusual friendship with Kim.

North Korea has continued with a series of missile launches that have ratcheted up tensions in the region. On Monday, it fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said. It marked Pyongyang's fourth ballistic missile test in about a month.

Trump's overtures to North Korea come at a delicate moment in US-South Korea relations, with the two countries at odds over trade and security.

The US president has threatened to hit South Korea with new trade penalties if it does not follow through with an investment in a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska, a $54 billion plan he has hailed as a centerpiece of Seoul's $350 billion investment commitment. The South Korean government has said it only agreed to the project if it proves economically viable.

In August, Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back military exercises with South Korea, citing his frustration that Seoul declined to support US military operations against Iran and saying the drills sent an "inappropriate signal" to North Korea.

articles.body: A passenger's trip through airport security lines took an unexpected turn after TSA officers noticed something unusual hidden inside a piece of computer equipment. The unidentified passenger was going through security at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport in Arizona when a TSA officer spotted on the X-ray machine an unusual mass and wiring inside an Apple Mac mini desktop computer. A closer inspection revealed suspected fentanyl, methamphetamine and ketamine concealed inside the manipulated computer, the TSA said in an Oct. 9 release. "When I found out it was drugs, I was very surprised." TSA Officer Isaiah Martinez Jr. then searched the carry-on and consulted with Stortz about the suspicious computer. Zelensky unleashes on Trump over Russia diesel deal

Kyiv’s allies, including those in President Trump’s circle, are rallying around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, pushing back against Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and threats to cut off weapons and intelligence sharing to Ukraine.

Zelensky, buoyed by the support, has unleashed criticism against Trump , calling the president “weak” for making a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. And he’s challenging Trump’s narrative over high diesel prices, pointing to the U.S. war with Iran as the main driver.

“Everybody understands that the prices of diesel, it doesn’t depend on our attacks on diesel in Russia,” Zelensky said in an interview with Fox News’s Bill Hemmer on Monday, addressing Trump’s favorite news channel during the morning hours, when he’s reportedly most likely to be watching.

“Everybody understands that it depends on the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.”

Zelensky’s indignation followed Trump’s announcement on Friday that he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an effort to lower prices in the U.S. — promoting the deal as a salve before the midterms as American voters fret over the cost of living.

Trump’s diesel deal drew immediate and wide-ranging pushback from Ukraine’s supporters.

Fox News host Mark Levin, who has a direct line to the president, said Putin is the actual obstacle to achieving peace in Eastern Europe and highlighted the Kremlin’s support for Iran in its conflict against the U.S.

Fox News host Brian Kilmeade, meanwhile, threw down over the weekend with co-host Rachel Campos-Duffy — who is married to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy — as she backed Trump’s criticism of Zelensky.

“It would be the biggest mistake of his administration to work with Russia,” Kilmeade said, speaking about the president.

articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has informed the employees that they will not receive the company’s usual annual salary hikes this year, as the company grapples with the increasing costs related to artificial intelligence and the uncertain business environment and global geopolitical challenges. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Vembu said that the outlook for the software industry remains uncertain and that AI has significantly increased operating expenses for companies such as Zoho. As per Vembu, the server prices required for data centers have surged four-fold, while increasing usage of AI tools has led to much higher expenses that the company is attempting to control. He also added that these pressures have been compounded by a challenging geopolitical backdrop.No salary hikes at Zoho this yearAs part of its efforts to manage costs, Zoho has reduced its marketing budget and paused annual salary increases for employees. Vembu said the decision was difficult and acknowledged that he had apologised to employees for not being able to avoid suspending pay hikes this year. The comments offer a rare glimpse into the financial pressures faced by software companies as they invest heavily in AI infrastructure while navigating an increasingly competitive technology landscape.We will work hard to avoid mass layoffs: Zoho founder Sridhar VembuWhile warning that the broader outlook for software jobs is "grim", Vembu stressed that Zoho is trying to avoid large-scale workforce reductions. "We will work hard to avoid mass layoffs," he said, even as he cautioned that employment prospects across the software sector are becoming more challenging.Vembu also revealed that Zoho has not increased its employee headcount for the last 18 months, signalling a prolonged hiring slowdown at the Chennai-headquartered software company.
